entry.title: Garmin Enduro 4 Everything You Need To Know: What’s Actually New?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

Garmin has announced the new Enduro 4, which takes the existing Enduro 3 and Fenix 9-ifies it. This follows the same pattern that Garmin did when it announced the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series back a few years ago. This means that the Enduro 4 gets some updated hardware internals, such as a faster processor and more RAM, as well as doubled storage for more offline maps. With those more powerful internals, you’re getting faster mapping features. Plus of course, the Enduro 4 gets all the Fenix 9 software features (which Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 users are also getting).

There are also some slight material changes too, mainly with the band and bezel. They’ve swapped out the UltraFit band for the new ComfortFit ones, which is a great change in my opinion. I’ve been using the new ComfortFit ones with the Fenix 9 series, and they’re awesome. Further, they changed up the color of the bezel, which you may or may not like depending on your personal color palette preferences.

In any case, I’ve started to put the Enduro 4 through its paces, though given all the other wearables slated for the next 6 days, wrist space is very limited right now. So for the moment, let’s just get into how things are different.

What’s New:

The Enduro 3 to Enduro 4 upgrade of hardware may not seem like a big one, mostly because you have to remember the whole point of the Enduro series is to *minimize* things that burn lots of battery. Meaning, adding in battery-hungry features like LTE & inReach (satellite messaging) are sorta the last thing you want Garmin to do.

However, more critical here is Garmin’s decision to bring virtually all the new Fenix 9 features back to the Fenix 8/8 Pro & Enduro 3 watches. Thus, by definition, with them all being treated as a single software platform, it becomes a more minor hardware update (akin to what Apple does each year). The point isn’t really for Enduro 3 owners to buy up (because you’re getting all the cool new Fenix 9 software features for free), but rather, for Enduro 1 & Enduro 2 folks to buy up. Make sense?

In any case, here’s what’s new hardware-wise:

– Faster processor for maps (specifically the Fenix 9 base processor, not the Fenix 9 Pro processor)
– 50% more RAM for map speed increases
– Doubled storage from 32GB to 64GB
– Went from black titanium bezel to a grey titanium bezel
– Cleaned up bezel to have fewer green/yellow markings
– Changed the GPS mode names to match Fenix 9, though the battery life remains identical
– Changed from UltraFit band to ComfortFit with QuickFit (trust me, it’s far better)
– New band increased total unit weight by 3g, case weight is identical (total weight from 63g to 66g)
– Same $899 price as the Enduro 3 (though the Enduro 3 went on sale this week to $799 with a bunch of other Garmin things for Amazon Prime Days)

Here you can see the new band/clasp system as part of the ComfortFit bands:

Meanwhile, here are the things that stay the same from Enduro 3 to Enduro 4:

– Same exact 1.4” MIP display panel at 280x280px
– Same exact Solar components
– Same exact smartwatch battery life (36 days smartwatch, 90 days with Solar)
– Same rough GPS battery life (see chart), though with new mode names
– Same thickness and case size (51mm)

Here’s the battery ‘chart’ showing all the battery modes/times:

Enduro 4 Battery Specs/Claims:
Smartwatch: Up to 36 days/90 days with solar*
Low Power Watch Mode: Up to 92 days/unlimited with solar*
Activity Mode (Normal): Up to 80 hours/144 hours with solar**
Activity Mode + Music (Normal): Up to 22 hours/25 hours with solar**
Activity Mode (Max Battery): Up to 210 hours/unlimited with solar**
Activity Mode (Extended Battery): Up to 120 hours/320 hours with solar**
Activity Mode (Max Accuracy): Up to 60 hours/90 hours with solar**
Expedition Mode: Up to 77 days/unlimited with solar*

*Solar charging, assuming all-day wear with 3 hours per day outside in 50,000 lux conditions
**Solar charging, assuming use in 50,000 lux conditions; assuming typical use with SatIQ technology

Here’s a side-by-side photo of the two units out tanning in the direct sun.

(At left, Enduro 3, at right Enduro 4)

Then, from a software standpoint, here are all the new features. All but the last few features are coming to the Enduro 3 via software update (in fact, some, like the Ski Erg features, already did last week). However, this just gets you all of them right now. The last few ones are dependent on the new mapping engine, which in turn requires the faster processor/more RAM:

– Added new Garmin Epic features, which group multi-day events/adventures (both on-device, and on Garmin Connect)
– New Stamina zone concept
– Added New Stamina Endurance time concept
– Added New Stamina trending feature (on Garmin Connect)
– Added New Running & Cycling Stamina graphs/curves
– Added New Rucking/Pack-Weight calorie breakout for activities (in multiple sport profiles)
– Revamped algorithms around pack-weight to more accurately cover calorie impacts
– Added New Rucking target calculator on-watch: Can tell you how far you need to go for a certain goal & pack weight
– Added ability to change pack-weight mid-activity
– Added Dedicated Rucking Reports (summarizing pack weight, calories, elevation, pace)
– Added Rucking Multisport mode option
– Added New on-device Rucking structured workouts with GoRuck
– Added New Ski Erg Profile (officially called ‘XC Ski Indoor’)
– Huge update/change for Indoor Rowing
– Added new heart rate zones for rowing, and max heart rate
– Added new power zones and power curves for running
– Added new indoor rowing FTP values/estimation
– Added new indoor rowing VO2Max values
– Added lactate threshold for rowing, and performance condition
– Added indoor rowing activity profile countdown timer (5-second timer, to let you get ready)
– Added support for indoor rowing to update Training Status (e.g., Productive, Unproductive, etc.)
– Added Rolling GAP as a data field (both kilometer and mile)
– Added Rolling GAP as a structured workout target option
– Added new ‘Field Tools’ feature, including ABC, measure height, reference point, and more

And then, here’s another set of new features that the Enduro 4 & Fenix 9 series get, but the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series won’t get, due to hardware constraints dependent on the increased RAM & processor (or, in the case of the GPS modes, so they don’t have to re-test all of the existing models’ official specs for new battery claims).

– Mapping: New Perspective view (sorta a tilted map view)
– Mapping Performance: Smoother/faster zoom
– Mapping Performance: More responsive heading updates (orientation)
– Added new ArcheryX feature
– Added new Dynamic Battery GPS modes, which basically simplify the naming of the satellite modes

Again, if you have an existing Garmin Enduro 3 or Fenix 8 series watch, you’ll eventually get all of the features in the first list. The timelines on that remain fuzzy, but Garmin says it won’t be this year for everything, though some features have already started showing up in recent updates.

Key Differences to Fenix 9?

(At left, Enduro 3, center Enduro 4, right Fenix 9 Pro Solar 47mm)

Now, real quick, what are the key differences between the Enduro 4 vs Fenix 9? Just like with the Enduro 3 vs Fenix 8 series, this is mostly about the Enduro series being optimized for higher battery life, but also reduced costs. They do away with extra things required for diving, LTE, speakers/mic, etc., and that in turn gives you more battery life and a ‘cheaper Fenix’ in the name of Enduro. Again, remember the Enduro & Fenix watches are under the same software watch family. All software releases for the Enduro 3 & Fenix 8 series were identical and grouped together, and the same is now true with the Enduro 4 & Fenix 9.

In any case, here are the key differences (when focused specifically on the SOLAR-MIP models):

– Enduro 4 has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar models
– Enduro 4 is far lighter than the Fenix 9 (66g vs 102g for the Fenix 9 Pro Solar 51mm non-inReach)
– Enduro 4 is slightly thinner than the Fenix 9 (15.7mm vs 16.6mm for Fenix 9 Pro Solar 51mm)
– Enduro 4 is offered in one size (51mm), whereas Fenix 9 is offered in three sizes (43/47/51mm, though MIP-Solar only in 47/51mm)
– Fenix 9 series has depth gauge and scuba/freediving features (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 series has induction buttons for better water resistance
– Fenix 9 series has a speaker/microphone (Enduro 4 has a simple beeper, no microphone
– Fenix 9 series has voice control/calling features with that microphone (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 Pro series has a faster processor than the Fenix 9 base/Enduro 4 units
– Fenix 9 Pro series has full Titanium case options (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 Pro series has a green LED flashlight (plus the white/red that Enduro 4 has)
– Fenix 9 Pro inReach models have LTE & inReach Satellite Message (Enduro 4 does not)
– Fenix 9 base starts at $999 (AMOLED only), Fenix 9 Pro from $1,099 (AMOLED/SOLAR), Fenix 9 Pro inReach/LTE from $1,199 (Enduro 4 is $899)

When it comes to those LTE & inReach Satellite features found on the Fenix 9 Pro inReach models, these are those features (none of which are on Enduro 4):

– LTE Live two-way voice calls
– LTE LiveTrack (30-second sampling rate)
– LTE Voice Messaging
– LTE Text Messaging
– LTE Weather
– LTE & Satellite Emergency SOS
– LTE Location Check-Ins
– LTE Incident Detection & Assistance
– Satellite Messaging (basic texting)
– Satellite position/location check-ins
– Satellite Emergency SOS (via Garmin Response)
– Satellite updating of weather (new in the Fenix 9 Pro)

In terms of some quick-hit similarities between the Enduro 4 and Fenix 9, this is things at a high level:

– Both run the same software and all the same features
– Both have Garmin’s Elevate Gen5 optical HR sensor
– Both have medically certified ECG hardware/features
– Both have Sapphire glass display covers (lens)
– Both have LED flashlights (but again, Fenix 9 Pro models have green LED too)
– Both have onboard offline maps
– Both have onboard storage for offline music (Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, MP3 files, etc.), to play back with Bluetooth headphones
– Both have WiFi syncing support
– Both have full ANT+ & Bluetooth Sensor support

Again, there are a gazillion more things that are the same between those two watches (primarily on the software side), but those are the main things to remember.

Mapping Speed Differences:

Now, with everything essentially being the same software-wise and display/battery-wise, the only real difference between the two is around the increased processing power, increased RAM, and then,  in turn,  the downstream improvements to map processing that Garmin has touted for the Enduro 4 as well as Fenix 9 series units.

Remember that in this case, the Enduro 4 shares the same processor as the base Fenix 9 units, not the slightly faster Fenix 9 Pro series processor. That new base processor is still faster than the Fenix 8 series units (which the Enduro 3 shared), and Garmin says a fair chunk of the improvements to speed is also coming from the rebuilt mapping engine, which requires that 50% improvement in RAM.

In any case, all that said, in terms of the speed improvements I see, like with the Fenix 9, it’s mostly ‘shrug’. Yes, they are faster, but not massively so. Here are some simple tests I did:

Speed test: Open a course file of 50KM/31mi:
Enduro 3: ~8 seconds
Enduro 4: ~8 seconds
Fenix 9 Pro: ~8 seconds

Speed test: Create a running route to a point across the island over a mountain range ( 23KM away as the bird flew, 30KM as the runner went):
Enduro 3: 1min 15sec
Enduro 4: 45sec
Fenix 9 Pro: 28sec

In the video, I also show some differences panning around, for which there is a notable difference, but mainly about 1-2 seconds of extra render time in my mountain-ish area with just light trails/terrain. Perhaps in some city scenario or such, but realistically that’s not where I tend to use the mapping features of any Garmin watch (I have my phone for that).

Now, as I noted in the Fenix 9 review, it’s easy to compare the maps from COROS zooming around/panning around, but the simple reality is those aren’t fully routable maps. They are essentially pictures/tiles that just load, whereas Garmin is actually rendering up a full routable map that you can route on-device to any other point without a phone. Creating a new route on a COROS device requires a phone. On an Amazfit device, you can create on-device routes only for round-trip routes, and even then, they almost always fail (as every reviewer has pointed out). Likewise, Garmin’s maps have far more information depth than anyone else.

Now, don’t mistake me pointing out map facts from me saying you actually need the on-device route generation that Garmin has in everyday life. As I noted in my Fenix 9 review, I can literally count on one hand the number of times in the real world I use the on-device route creation in real life (aside for review funsies purposes) as roughly twice. And neither time was super critical. Handy, yes…critical no.

In just the same way that while I don’t find that feature super useful, neither do I find just randomly panning around the map like a candy-fueled toddler, like every YouTuber likes to do. I simply don’t do that in real life out on multi-day treks, or even long single-day ultras. Do I occasionally check something a few hundred meters away? Sure. Does it take an extra 1-2 seconds on a Garmin? Sure. Am I upset that I have to wait 1-2 seconds longer in the middle of a 17-hour day? Nah. Do I wish Garmin’s maps were faster? Of course.

All of these things can be true. It doesn’t have to be fanboyism.

In any event, one new mapping feature is the new Perspective View, as seen on the Fenix 9. Here’s what that looks like side-by-side with the Enduro 3’s straight-down view:

(At left, Enduro 3, at right Enduro 4)

I’ve grown to like this view quite a bit on the Fenix 9, though admittedly, half the time I forget to tap the little compass icon to toggle it on. Plus, I don’t tend to stay on the mapping page for very long, since the mapping page on every watch is the fastest way to see just how little battery life you’ll actually get (map pages burn battery life like crazy on every wearable).

Wrap-Up:

Ultimately, the Enduro 4 is one of those Garmin upgrades that really isn’t about appealing to the prior-gen owners. Just like most Apple Watch upgrades aren’t about appealing to people who just bought last year. Instead, it’s primarily targeted at existing Enduro 1 or Enduro 2 owners who would get a big boost in terms of sports features as well as daily life things. And I suppose, for those who simply want the new Fenix 9 features now, versus waiting for Garmin to release those planned updates to the existing Enduro 3 owners.

While some might want even longer battery life, or perhaps a better MIP display, or perhaps changes in solar – the reality is that those are all industry-leading within the category in real-world usage. The Enduro 4 (and Enduro 3 before it) already has the longest GPS battery life out there, even before solar gains are considered, which can push it notably higher. As for the MIP displays, the reality is that there are very few companies making these panels, and they have very little reason to innovate in an area that continues to see dwindling unit volume. Certainly, I’d love to see a more readable MIP display in dimmer conditions, but I have a feeling that’s not happening anytime soon. Especially as AMOLED watch unit overall battery life continues to climb closer and closer to MIP display units.

In any event, assuming you’re choosing a MIP display unit, between the Garmin Enduro 4 vs Enduro 3 vs Fenix 9, I think the question you ask yourself is relatively simple: Do you care about scuba diving, microphone/speaker features, LTE, Satellite Communications, or a smaller 43/47mm unit? If the answer to all of those is ‘Nah’, then the Enduro is the clear winner. If you go for the Enduro 4, you’ll save yourself $200 over the Fenix 9 Solar unit priced at $1,099+. If you want to save a bit, you could pick up the Enduro 3 at a bit cheaper today, knowing it’ll get virtually all those new Enduro 4 software features in a few months or so. What the future in a year or two brings, I’ve got no idea (and I suspect Garmin hasn’t decided yet either).

In any case, hopefully all the above was useful in helping you decide.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: Carlo’s Cascada x Massacan Pianella MTB
entry.content:
For this week’s Readers’ Rides, we have a follow-up to John’s Shop Visit with Massacan in Nice, France, and that special one-of-one Pianella frame painted for Italian apparel company Cascada. Read on Carlo from Cascada’s words on this special Pianella MTB collaboration…

I wanted to send you our custom Cascada x Massacan Pianella for Readers’ Rides.

Funny enough, you already saw the frame before we did :-) When you visited Lucie, Matt and the Massacan crew in Nice this summer, the freshly painted Cascada frame was there with them, so you had a first look at it before it even made its way back to us in Italy.

The story behind the bike actually started a few years earlier.

At the end of 2022, French illustrator Denis Carrier, a longtime collaborator of Cascada, who has designed several graphics for us over the years, introduced us to Lucie and Massacan, which at the time was still a young project taking shape in the South of France.

Lucie got in touch while they were preparing the launch of their first bikes. The idea was simple: head out on a multi-day bikepacking trip between France and Italy and involve Cascada in the project.

Their bikes were being welded and painted in Italy, not far from Lake Garda, where we live, and the connection felt immediate.

My answer at the time was basically: count on us.

At Cascada, we’ve always been drawn to collaborations that start from the ground up: projects where two independent brands can ride together, create something together and grow alongside each other, rather than simply place two logos on the same product.

That first email became the beginning of a friendship and an ongoing collaboration.

Over the following years, Massacan bikes found their way to our part of the Italian Alps, where we rode them through our mountains, forests and trails. We worked together on photo shoots, trips and projects, while Denis Carrier also designed Cascada x Massacan Trail T-shirts and bandanas.

Last May, we spent two days together in Val di Ledro (North Italy), for The Lodge Dispatch, an event we organized around the presentation of our SS2026 collection. We stayed at a lodge deep in the woods, rode together, introduced the Pianella and the rest of the Massacan bikes to the Italian cycling community and shared the new Cascada collection in the same setting.

Before the event, Lucie and Matt came to us with an idea: they asked if we wanted to design a Cascada graphic for a Pianella frame and make the bike ours.

It was an easy yes.

The finished bike was then delivered to us during the event in Val di Ledro.

The result is this Massacan Pianella, assembled for us by Matt at Massacan and finished with a custom paint job by Tony Spray.

The Pianella is an adventure hardtail: Massacan’s first mountain bike and its first steel frame, built around Columbus Zona tubing. For ours, we chose a rigid Columbus Futura Adventure carbon fork and a simple, capable build suited to the kind of riding we do most: forest trails, mountain tracks, long days outside and the occasional bikepacking trip.

What makes this one particularly personal is the frame.

We designed the complete graphic treatment ourselves at Cascada and asked Tony Spray to bring it to life. Rather than creating a conventional co-branded paint scheme, we treated the frame almost like a blank canvas.

The sand, olive and burnt-orange palette comes directly from the colors and landscapes surrounding Cascada. Across the frame we added symbols that have become part of our visual language over the years: the moon, the sun, the snake, wildlife and the words Stay Wild.

They are small references to the things that have always shaped Cascada: mountains, forests, rivers, travelling slowly and the ongoing search for unknown places.

Even the bike carries traces of the relationship behind it: Cascada x Massacan on the top tube, Massacan’s handwritten Pianella lettering and Tony Spray’s signature on the frame.

For us, it’s much more than a custom-painted bike.

It’s probably the clearest physical expression of everything that grew out of that first email in 2022: French ideas, Italian craftsmanship, independent brands, shared rides and a lot of time spent together on dirt roads.

And, most importantly, it’s a bike that gets ridden.

Build Spec:

  • Frame: Massacan Pianella — Columbus Zona steel
  • Fork: Columbus Futura Adventure carbon
  • Assembly: Matt / Massacan
  • Custom paint: Tony Spray
  • Rear derailleur: Shimano Deore XT RD-M8100, 12-speed
  • Cassette: Shimano Deore XT CS-M8100, 12-speed
  • Brakes: Shimano Deore XT M8100 hydraulic disc
  • Wheelset: Miche 988 WHS, 29″
  • Hubs: Miche
  • Tires: Vittoria Barzo XC-Trail, 29 x 2.25″
  • Handlebar: Ritchey Trail
  • Stem: Ritchey
  • Seatpost: Crankbrothers dropper
  • Saddle: Selle San Marco Mantra
  • Pedals: Shimano PD-ED500 SPD
  • Bottle cages: Ritchey Classic Steel

See more of the Pianella at Massacan.

 

 

We’d like to thank all of you who submitted Readers Rides builds to be shared here at The Radavist. The response has been incredible, and we have so many to share over the next few months. Feel free to submit your bike, listing details, components, and other information. You can also include a portrait of yourself with your bike and your Instagram account! Please shoot landscape-orientation photos, not portrait. Thanks!

entry.title: Gear Up for Foul-Weather Riding
entry.content:
Endura’s Scottish homeland gets every kind of weather, even sunshine. Far more common, though, are the seemingly infinite combinations of blustery, bracing, and wet that give the Scots language its uncommonly rich collection of weather words. 

We should expect nothing less of a country ribbed with ancient hills reminiscent of Appalachia, flowing into rugged seascapes worthy of Coastal California, and bathed in the light-sucking drizzle of Southeast Alaska. Cyclists, of course, will recognize all those places for their world-class roads, gravel and singletrack. Which brings us to the quandary that gave us Endura’s lineup of foul-weather kit: When the trail is braw, but the weather is dreich, what is a cyclist to do? 

Suit up and ride, of course*. With the proper Endura kit you’ll finish your trail day well and fully chuffed, and nae the least bit oorlich.

*Assuming the trails aren’t closed; always follow the direction of your local trail Org.

AllTrack Race Cape

The AllTrack Race Cape packs serious rain protection into an ultralight shell built for road and gravel duty. How serious? The cape sports a 20,000mm waterproof rating, which is how scientists say it can hold back a 65-foot column of water. That plus fully taped seams means this compact and packable bit of foul weather kit goes anywhere and is ready for anything. 

Shop Now

SingleTrack Windproof Glove 

The SingleTrack Windproof Glove blocks the chill with a softshell backhand and lightly brushed lining for knuckle protection without bulky insulation. A zero-padding synthetic-leather palm and silicone grip preserve bar feel, while the Velcro cuff locks down the fit.

Shop Now

Endura AllTrack Rout Pant

Built for riders who don’t need their trail pants painted on, the AllTrack Rout Pant uses four-way stretch fabric and a relaxed fit with room for knee pads. Articulated, tapered legs keep things pedal-friendly, while a DWR finish, adjustable waist, and zipped pockets handle everyday trail duty.

Shop Now

Endura AllTrack Roam WP Jacket

The AllTrack Roam WP Jacket adds a bombproof outer layer to Endura’s AllTrack line of relaxed ride-anything-anytime gear. Stretch construction gives you room to move on technical trails, keeping the rain and smirr at bay without the restrictive feel of a race shell. 

Shop Men’s Shop Women’s

Endura MT500 Burner Fleece 

More technical midlayer than bulky winter top, the MT500 Burner Fleece warms your upper body and sleeves with Polartec Alpha insulation. Pit zips dump excess heat, while the four-way stretch and relaxed Roam fit give you freedom to move when the trails get touzie.

Shop Now

Endura MT500 Roam Insulated Jacket

For those pure Baltic trail days, the MT500 Roam Insulated Jacket backs up a two-layer, water-repellent DWR outer with breathable Polartec Alpha insulation. Underarm vents allow excess heat to escape, while articulated sleeves, roomy front pockets, and an adjustable hood make this a versatile layer for those unforgettable winter rips.

Shop Now

AllTrack Roam Fleece

Constructed of breathable fabric and a soft fleece interior, the AllTrack Roam Fleece wraps you in a warm embrace without smothering hard efforts, while articulated sleeves maintain riding mobility. A relaxed Roam fit and zippered valuables pocket provide the sort of style and practicality that will make this midlayer a favorite on and off the bike. 

Shop Now

Endura AllTrack Ride L/S Jersey 

Part jersey, part adventure shirt, the AllTrack Ride L/S blends a lightweight merino-knit body with stretchy ripstop sleeves for added trail durability. Articulated sleeves improve riding fit, while three rear drop-in pockets and a zippered security pocket provide road-jersey utility without the road-racer aesthetic.

Shop Men’s Shop Women’s

This article is sponsored by Endura.

entry.title: The Crankbrothers Trail Speed Lace Seal Are For Wet Season Riding
entry.content:
The wet, rainy, and cold season is approaching, and in areas where it’s ok to ride muddy trails, keeping your feet dry can be an ordeal. Crankbrothers‘ new Trail Speed Lace Seal shoes are designed for wet, cold rides. Its all-new Seal shoe lineup is engineered to keep you riding well into the off-season. The silhouette features reflective hits for visibility when riding at dusk. With a waterproof membrane and a unique 360° ankle wrap to keep the elements out, these Seal shoes keep you comfortable when conditions get uncomfortable.

Available in clipless ($229.99) or flat pedal ($209.99) at Crankbrothers.com or your local dealer.

entry.title: NOBL Ethos SL MTB Wheelset is 1079g with Tape & Valves, and It’s Not Even Their Lightest
entry.content:
There’s no shortage of aftermarket wheels out there, so that’s forcing brands to figure out ways to stand out in the crowd. For NOBL, that means hand-building wheels in Cumberland, BC, for Canadian customers or in Bellingham, WA, for the Americans. While those wheels cover a wide range of disciplines and styles, NOBL seems to be planting its flag as a premier builder of ultra-lightweight wheels with the help of BERD spokes.

Wheels like the Ethos SL would certainly qualify. Which makes it even more amazing when you consider that these aren’t even the lightest that they offer. Built with a 29″ rim that measures 30mm internally and 20.5mm deep, the Ethos SL gets a pair of NOBL’s own TI70 hubs that were designed in conjunction with BERD and Erase Components out of Belgium.

The hubs are hooked so they offer a perfect mount for the looped BERD spoke ends and provide 5.14º of engagement. The Ti part of the name hints at the titanium freehub, and the 70 references the 70t ratchet. Hubs are offered in either 6-bolt or centerlock with HG, MicroSpline, or XD freehub options.

Each wheel is built with 28 BERD Polylight Dyneema spokes which loop around the hub and attach to a rim with standard Sapim Alloy Secure Lock nipples that thread onto the stainless steel threaded section bonded to the end of the spoke.

The BERD spokes are a big part of the lightweight story, but far from the only part. Compared to the NOBL Ethos XC wheelset, which is said to have a reinforced layup that is 21% stronger, the Ethos SL rims opt for an ultralight carbon layup with T800 and T1000 carbon fiber (and a 2mm taller rim profile than the XC rims). Calling them their lightest rim ever, the 270g SL rims are hookless with a 2.9mm-wide rim bead that’s angled and reinforced with a “flexible material” to make them more durable and impact-resistant.

On our scale with rim tape and NOBL’s own valve stems installed, the actual weights come out to 489g for the front and 590g for the rear. Just 1079g for the pair. If you need something lighter, the Ethos SL180 drops to a claimed 993g for the pair thanks to DT Swiss 180 hubs.

Unfortunately for us, by the time these wheels showed up, the bike I had intended to use them on had to go back, and the freehub wasn’t right for any other bike I had to test them on, so we didn’t get any time on them before the wheels themselves had to go back to NOBL.

Overall, though, the NOBL Ethos SL wheels are a very interesting option if you’re looking for an insanely light set of 29″ wheels. Like the old adage goes, “light, strong, cheap, pick two…” you will definitely not find the Ethos SL to be cheap. The SLs sell for $2,399 for a set, with options for glossy white, gold, silver, and black decals included. The Ethos XC wheels are only $100 less for a 1,175g claimed weight, but with a stronger rim as mentioned. Or go the other way with the Ethos SL180s priced at $2,799. All NOBL rims include a lifetime warranty for the original owner, so long as it fails “while being used as intended.”

noblwheels.com

entry.title: Review: Giro’s New Montaro Pro is a Near-Perfect Mountain Bike Helmet
entry.content:
Giro introduced the Montaro Pro back in mid-August, replacing the longstanding Manifest Spherical as the top-of-the-line half-shell in its MTB helmet lineup. With this new lid, Giro has consolidated its mid- and top-tier helmets under the somewhat iconic Montaro name. While design features and elements of the Manifest carry over, they also gave it bolder, more angular styling that aligns more consistently with the design language of its more affordable sibling, the Montaro III.

I’ve been testing the new Giro Montaro Pro since it became available a couple of months ago. I’ve been wearing it on mountain bike rides and eMTB rides, in hot weather and in cooler temperatures, and so far, so good. Well, mostly. I think the Montaro Pro is damn near perfect, but there’s just one thing holding it back from greatness.

Giro Montaro Pro

Check Price at Performance Bike

Specifications

  • MSRP: $300
  • Weight: 465 g (Medium)
  • Rotational Impact Protection System: Mips Spherical
  • Adjustable visor: Yes
  • Number of vents: 23
  • Available sizes: S, M, L
  • Virginia Tech Helmet Safety Rating: Not rated

Pros

  • Very comfortable
  • Well-ventilated
  • Mips Spherical design seems effective
  • NTA e-bike certified
  • Fidlock buckle
  • Looks pretty good

Cons

  • Expensive
  • Visor doesn't block low sun angles
  • Not test by Virginia tech
Jeremy Benson

Montaro Pro Review

As mentioned above, the Montaro Pro carries over some of the features of the Manifest Spherical it replaces, with a bolder style closer to the Montaro III. It’s positioned as the top-tier half-shell mountain bike helmet in Giro’s lineup, with the $299.95 price tag to match. You can learn the details in our first look coverage here.

Fit and Comfort

Giro has been making mountain bike helmets for decades, and I’ve always gotten along really well with the way they fit. That continues with the Montaro Pro, which seems to fit almost exactly like its predecessor, the Manifest. That is to say, I find it’s perfectly neutral compared to POC helmets, for example, which are slightly narrower in my experience. It fits my average/oval shaped head well, and I think it should work for most riders. Those with outlier head shapes would still be wise to try it on to be sure, of course.

As with most helmets, my 59cm head circumference lands me squarely on the cusp of the medium (55-59) and large (59-63) shell sizes. This leaves me squeezing into a medium or swimming in a large. I went with the medium, and I think that was the right choice. Even at the upper end of its fit range, the shell drops down pretty low on the sides and back of the head given its relatively deep fit. 

Inside, the padding is relatively plush across the brow and top of the head. Giro’s RocLoc Trail Air adjustment system has three stages of height adjustment and a large dial that’s easy to twist with or without gloves when adding or removing tension. In my opinion, it’s one of the more user-friendly and comfortable fit adjustment systems on the market. 

I also appreciate the adjustable strap cradle by the ears. Not only does it hold them flat, but it keeps them from making any unwanted contact with my lobes, and it’s adjustable if needed. The single webbing strap under the chin is also unobtrusive, and the Fidlock buckle is quick and easy to use. 

Protection

I don’t have any helmet impact testing equipment, so I can only judge the Montaro Pro and any other helmets I test based on what I perceive to be their protective qualities. We’ve also come to rely on Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ratings to provide comparative impact test ratings, but unfortunately, the Montaro Pro has not been tested. Of course, it meets all of the standard helmet safety requirements for its CPSC certification. It has also been tested for higher speeds up to 28 mph and is NTA-8776 e-bike certified. 

On my head, the Montaro Pro has a relatively deep fit and extended coverage over the occipital lobe and temples that’s typical of modern trail helmets. It’s stable and secure and has a sturdy, reassuring feel before even considering features like Aura II structural reinforcement. 

I’ve worn Giro’s Aries Spherical and Manifest Spherical helmets previously, and the dual-shell Mips Spherical design seems like it should be highly effective. The upper and lower shells move independently of each other and are quite easy to shift around by hand. I’m just basing this assessment on feel (or maybe vibes), but it feels more protective than a thin plastic liner or Mips integrated into helmet padding. In my experience, the Spherical design doesn’t make any annoying noises either.

Ventilation

The Montaro Pro has 23 Wind Tunnel Vents that provide solid ventilation. I wouldn’t call it class-leading, but I’m actually impressed with how much air moves over my head given the dual-shell Mips Spherical design. It’s most noticeable and effective at the front of the helmet, where air flows directly to my forehead through the large front vents. Shallow air flow channels do a commendable job of moving that air from front to back.

Given the fairly shallow depth of the internal airflow channels, however, the Montaro Pro is bested by a few others in the ventilation department. A couple of helmets I’ve tried recently that come to mind are the POC Cularis and the Specialized Ambush 3, both of which have significantly deeper airflow channels inside. 

Eyewear Storage

The two smallest vents on the brow of the Montaro Pro double as eyewear storage. I usually keep my sunglasses on my eyes while I’m riding, so I’m not a stickler for this feature. But on some particularly sweaty rides recently, I’ve stashed my shades on the climbs to keep sweat from dripping on my lenses. In my opinion, the spacing of these vents/slots is pretty ideal, making them easy to locate and insert the sunglass arms, even while riding. 

They also don’t feel like they’re stretching my sunglasses in the name of stability and security. The sunglasses I’ve tried have stayed put just fine, even over bumpy mountain trails. That said, the glasses sit an inch or so in front of the helmet shell, so they are in your field of view when stashed on the helmet.

Visor

In my opinion, a functional visor is one of the most important features of a mountain bike helmet. I’ve even gone so far as to rant it about. Prior to even receiving the Montaro Pro, I was skeptical of its two position adjustable visor based on looks alone. At first, when the sun angles were higher, I didn’t take much issue with it. Now that it’s fall and the sun angle creeps lower and lower each day, its given me something to complain about. 

The Montaro Pro’s visor has two positions. The high position provides plenty of room for goggle wearers needing to stash them on the helmet between laps. It also slides down into the low position, where the tip of the visor is just barely out of my field of view. Honestly, not having the visor in my peripheral vision whatsoever is pretty ideal most of the time. But as soon as I need it to block the sun from shining directly in my eyes, it requires that I angle my head downward to do so. 

Mid-summer or riding in a deep dark forest, it’s not a big deal. But at sunrise, sunset, or pretty much any time of day from October to March, another lower visor position would be very welcome. And given that it’s already adjustable, why not have another, lower position? Now, I recognize that I’m extra particular about visors because quite a bit of my local riding is in the high desert with limited tree cover. If you ride in the lush, shady forests of the Northeast or Pacific Northwest, this may not be an issue for you at all.

Weight

My size medium Montaro Pro weighs in at 465 grams on my scale. That puts it at the upper end of the weight spectrum compared to other half shell helmets I’ve tested. For comparison, the next heaviest helmets I’ve tried recently are the POC Cularis (440 grams), the Specialized Ambush 3 (441 grams), and the Smith Payroll (448 grams), all in size large.

While it might have a few grams on those helmets, it’s definitely not something I notice and the Montaro Pro does not feel heavy on my head. It carries its weight well, perhaps because of the great fit.

My Takeaway

Giro’s Montaro Pro is the evolution of its popular Manifest Spherical helmet, and I like nearly everything about it. It’s comfortable and has a protective feel with great coverage, the Mips Spherical rational impact protection system, and the NTA-8776 e-bike certification. It’s relatively well-ventilated, and I really like the way it looks, too.

My only real complaint is the visor, which is not the most effective at blocking the sun at low angles. That’s really the only flaw I’ve found in what is otherwise a near-perfect mountain bike helmet. It’ll be out of my rotation for a while, but it’ll be back in action once the sun is higher in the sky. The importance of visors varies, of course, and if it’s not a priority for you, the Montaro Pro is absolutely worth checking out. 

giro.com

entry.title: A Wet Time in the Woods with Dillen and Emerson: Bikepacking from Bellingham to Whistler – Paul Kalifatidi
entry.content:
Dillen Wilder lost his foot in a cycling accident, but not his love of the ride. Since moving to Bellingham, Washington, he’s found recovery, friendship, and a new perspective in the Heavy Bike Club, a judgment-free crew that favors the bikes they love over the newest, lightest gear. Dillen shares how that mindset led him and his friend Emerson to load up their steel hardtails and ride nearly 200 miles through relentless Pacific Northwest rain, all to get to the Whistler Bike Park. It’s a story about sustainability, community, and the idea that the ride to the trailhead might be the best part of all.

The Heavy Bike Club

After losing my foot in a cycling accident, I moved in with my family to be closer to the kind of medical care and support I’d need as I learned to navigate life as an amputee. The community I found in this new city has been vital to my recovery; as essential as any doctor. While I developed a new relationship with bikes, I gravitated toward a cycling niche that might seem counterintuitive for a fella with mobility challenges: the Heavy Bike Club. Defined by folks who choose what they have and love over shiny new lightweight gear, the Heavy Bike Club is an intentionally judgement-free space for people to show up as they are and ride any distance. I found folks who did not seem to mind if I needed to take a break. No one rolled their eyes if I slowed down the group. My new friends are excited to be out on bikes and connecting with their local environment.

We are lucky here in Bellingham to have Kim and Andrew, owners of the local bike/coffee shop Cafe Velo. They are the humble unofficial figureheads of our Heavy Bike Club. It’s a motley group of individuals who certainly don’t mind riding a little slower to soak up extra moments on long summer days. They ride their own heavy bikes, and always encourage me when I’m dreaming up some new alterations to my own steel creations. Oh yeah, I build my own bikes.

Confused Looks

At first glance, the cycling community in Bellingham appears dominated by mountain bikers. Some, like me, would fall into the Heavy Bike Club with their older frames and (by industry standards) outdated components. Many would say they have other priorities. You may know the type: those with the newest carbon enduro bikes who drive their truck to the trailhead and rip hot laps with the boys. They cap their ride with a little “Vitamin R” (that’s Rainier beer for the uninitiated) in the parking lot. Some of these folks would never consider commuting by bike, or even riding a bike in a situation that doesn’t require knee pads. Not throwing shade, just describing the best-catered-to demographic in the Bellingham cycling industry. I love a “send train” down the jump line as much as the next mountain biker. However, I also adore steel hardtails. The bikes that are far more focused on the feel of the ride rather than the top speed of the ride. The bikes that draw confused looks from many at my local trailhead.

Steel is Sustainable

One of the biggest draws toward a steel hardtail for me is sustainability. A steel bicycle frame can outlive its original owner. When humanity comes to an end, a steel bicycle frame will slowly oxidize into dust and provide important nutrients for whatever critters that live on after our demise. That might be an odd thing to think about when choosing one’s preferred method of recreation, but these are things I think about.

I have been lucky to spend time in many corners of the cycling industry; from mass production to niche bespoke fabrication. One thing that stuck with me from my time working in factories was the volume of waste. Bicycles are routinely touted as green transportation, and an excellent way to stay fit while helping our ailing ecosystem. Yet here I was throwing away single-use foam bags used to protect high-end carbon components for assembly into high-end carbon bicycles. That was hard to justify in my mind. What about the future critters after the death of society? Where would they get their iron oxide if everyone is riding bikes made with synthetic epoxies that won’t gracefully degrade and feed the ecosystem?

Though in all seriousness, when I learned of wireless shifters built to be tossed once the battery dies, my head started spinning. Who asked for that? Products made and sold just because they can be. I feel like Dr. Ian Malcom in Jurassic Park saying, “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.” Do I have a solution for the continuous push towards new and “better” just because we can? No. I don’t think I can stop consumerism any more than I can stop asteroids from colliding with our planet. However, I do think it’s essential for cyclists, wherever they sit on the spectrum, to ask ourselves why we like to ride.

How does it improve cycling to build bigger parking lots at local trailheads? As an adaptive athlete, I love seeing accessible parking spaces at trailheads. I applaud making trails accessible for electric mountain bikes to get more folks out there on trails I love dearly. Riding IS for everyone, after all. Finding community in the cycling world is a wonderful experience that I want everyone to have. However, at what point is “more” actually improving the experiences we have on bikes?

An Ugly Flower

Pondering these questions planted a weird seed in my head. On the first weekend of June, this seed grew into a misshapen, foul-smelling, yet glorious flower.

Mountain biking was my first love. I’ve had more than one friend insinuate I am in an abusive relationship with mountain biking considering how much physical and emotional strife it has put me through. Yet I always come crawling back for more. When I discovered the joys of bikepacking, my relationship with mountain biking found more depth and beauty. In fact, I proselytize bikepacking a little too much to anyone who will stick around long enough to listen.

So one day, while at work in one of Bellingham’s many bike shops, that little seed in my head sprouted when I told my co-worker, “Wouldn’t it be cool to ride from here to Whistler Bike Park and do a few laps?” The ultimate “let’s just ride to the trailhead” experience.

Just Ride to the Trailhead

I love riding my mountain bike to our local trailheads here in Bellingham. But to a bike park? That was a crazy thought. To my delight, my co-worker gave an emphatic “YES.” This co-worker, Emerson, used to race downhill competitively and is a talented bike mechanic. This amazing lad undoubtedly knows his way around a bike. Last year, we designed and built him a rowdy custom hardtail that he’s been ripping around on for months now. He has thus slowly dipped his toes into the Heavy Bike Club. Seems he likes the vibes. So, we started scheming.

We would ride our steel hardtails, with everything we would need strapped to them, from my house in Bellingham to the Whistler Bike Park. All the while hitting as much singletrack along the way as we had the energy for. Just ride to the trailhead.

Our route changed many times after that first conversation. Out-of-date intel and overzealous bites of challenging singletrack eventually led us to the final route. Poor Emerson had never ridden more than 70-ish miles on any bike ever, let alone a loaded mountain bike. Yet he performed admirably. He embraced his newfound Heavy Bike Club label and helped me through this wild adventure. Even though I’ve put in more miles bikepacking, he’s much faster. Every time he came back to help me lift my heavy bike over a steep rooted section of singletrack, it filled me with joy to be out there with my friend. I’m so happy that we did this crazy thing together. Every step of the way, we made decisions together and embraced the bonkers conditions we got ourselves into. That is what it feels like to be accepted and embraced in your community. Working together towards a common goal is a beautiful thing, even if that goal is pretty absurd.

Bikepacking from Bellingham to Whistler

It took us three days to ride from Bellingham to Whistler, and it was the worst weather window in months. When we weren’t actively being rained on, we were chasing ominous grey skies. We had originally planned on cowboy camping. Mother Nature had other plans. With the added weight of our full tents, we rode off into the rain on a Sunday morning, lacing together dozens of miles of Bellingham’s greenways as we went deeper into Whatcom County. Quickly we found ourselves on an overgrown singletrack through the woods. This early assault by blackberry thorns set the scene for our shenanigans to come.

We rode and hiked our bikes for days through overgrown, washed-out, and muddy trails or roads with one unexpected detour after another. We rode at least one blue-rated singletrack per day while on our way up to the bike park (Noodley Appendage, CRC, and Man Boobs, for those curious). I could talk about the laughter and heartbreak for hours. The biggest takeaway? I had a blast mountain biking with my friend. I got to share my love of bikepacking with him. Stopping to look at cool trees and huge banana slugs while snacking on weird foods that just so happened to have the right form factor to fit in our bags. All the while smelling like a wet dog that may have rolled in something dead while you weren’t looking. (We never did dry out with the amount of rain we encountered; it was a truly Pacific Northwest experience.) Then, when we reached our destination, Emerson got to share with me some of his favorite lift-access trails. A melding of worlds. We embraced each other’s style of cycling and found a way to combine them.

To top it off, after almost 200 miles and over 20,000 feet of elevation gain got us just south of Whistler Village, we hitched the final few miles. A kind fellow dirtbag named Martin offered us a lift in the pouring rain. Those last few miles in Martin’s beat-up old pickup were glorious. He dropped us in the village and said he hoped we enjoyed our laps at the bike park. Thanks, Martin!

We rode our bikes to the trailhead (mostly). What is usually a three-hour drive, we turned into three days of moist mountain biking on quirky steel bikes. All of that for three amazing laps of the Whistler Bike Park. Did we reroute the onslaught of consumerism away from destroying our beloved natural spaces? Absolutely not. Did we offset our waste in a reasonable way? Almost certainly not. However, we did blow quite a few minds along the way. Every trail user who stopped to chat was amazed at the journey. Just a simple ride to the trailhead.

Do It Yourself

So, please, give it a try. Let your mind visit those strange recesses when thinking about the ecological impact of your choices. Or, if you don’t want to burden yourselves with the fate of the natural world, just go have fun on a ride with some cool people. Build community. Next time you are going for a mountain bike ride, give thought as to how you could make the ride to your favorite trails more memorable. Invite a friend. Maybe stop at the local taqueria, or maybe you will discover a new urban trail on the way there. This beautiful world is full of surprises. Some of them are delightful, and some of them are devastating. Seeing what is around the next corner is exciting regardless. Whatever is around that corner, though, we are in it together. I am going to keep riding to the trailhead every chance I get. I guess they were onto something when they said the journey is more important than the destination. Hope to see you out there!

The post A Wet Time in the Woods with Dillen and Emerson: Bikepacking from Bellingham to Whistler appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: COROS Pace 4 Pro In-Depth Review: Worth the Upsell?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The COROS Pace 4 Pro at first glance might just look like a premium materials Pace 4, and in many ways, there’s a fair bit of truth to that. And there’s nothing wrong with that, as I’ll dive into. It’s unquestionably a more premium watch than either the Pace 4 or Pace Pro, and it’s got a new heart rate sensor too (don’t worry, plenty of accuracy testing below).

But from a company standpoint, it represents a clear attempt at trying to break into the premium market. Less ‘trying to make’, and more ‘trying to get people to buy it’. While COROS continually smashes it out of the park when it comes to budget watches (e.g., the Pace 3 and most recently the Pace 4), it has repeatedly struggled to attract buyers to more premium-priced devices that compete head-to-head on price with Garmin. After all, it’s been 5 years since the last major launch of their top-end flagship COROS Vertix 2 (and no, I don’t count the slight materials refresh in the Vertix 2S as a major new watch, and even that was 2.5 years ago).

With the COROS Pace 4 Pro at $449, COROS is trying to thread the line just enough under Garmin’s premium pricing of the Forerunner 570 (at $549) to entice buyers to forget the FR570’s extra software features, and save the cash for ice cream. The question is, does COROS pull it off?

With that, let’s dive into it!

What’s New:

In some ways, it’s hard to have a ‘What’s New’ section when COROS doesn’t have a prior-generation Pace 3 Pro to compare it to. Instead, this watch is basically a re-imagined COROS Pace Pro, but with the ‘4’ stuck in there to keep marketing life simple. Though, it gains some features the Pace 4 added that the Pace Pro lacked.

There, here’s how it differs from the existing Pace Pro:

– Larger 1.47” AMOLED display from 1.3” AMOLED (biggest COROS screen to date)
– Increased pixels (466x466px vs previous 416x416px)
– Increased brightness to 3,500 nits (Pace 4 was 1,500 nits)
– Ability to add up to 11 data fields per page (from 8 fields on Pace Pro)
– Added new multi-data page field that can cram in 13 data fields
– New 4th Gen optical HR sensor (for COROS watch with it)
– Added sapphire glass display
– Added action button (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added microphone (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added voice control from watch (Pace Pro doesn’t have that, though Pace 4 does)
– Added full speaker (neither Pace Pro nor Pace 4 had that)
– Added ability to take calls from watch (neither Pace Pro nor Pace 4 had that)
– Added GPS ‘Auto’ mode (dynamically selects required satellite level)
– Increased maximum GPS battery from 38 hours to 60 hours
– Improved bezel material from plastic to titanium
– Increased weight from 32.5g to 38g
– Doubled the onboard RAM
– Same 22mm band size (same as Pace 3/4, Pace Pro, APEX 2 Pro, APEX 4 42mm)
– Priced at $449USD, 449EUR, $799AUD, 389GBP, 619CAD

From a software standpoint, there are actually no new software features here. At least unique/specific to the Pace 4 Pro. Instead, all the COROS watches are getting their usual roughly quarterly update of software features, and the Pace 4 Pro is part of that (as is the Pace Pro). For example, for September this included an update to the Adventure Journal (mostly on-app), the option to directly transfer firmware via computer, and cycling climb alerts on the watch (previously this was on Dura). Also recently there was a revamped sleep score and sleep metrics on the COROS app.

In terms of color options, there’s black and white, each with either the silicone or nylon straps:

In terms of all the other usual bits for recent COROS watches, it’s got:

– Global offline mapping pre-installed (and free downloadable updates)
– Turn-by-turn navigation with pre-planned route
– Barometric altimeter
– Dual-frequency/multiband GNSS/GPS
– 32GB of Storage
– 447 mAh battery capacity
– 5ATM (50m) water resistance
– Access to the COROS MCP for connecting to Claude & ChatGPT

Next, looking at the size, here’s how things compare:

Also, importantly, the display itself is identical in size to that of an Oreo. Concerned about accuracy, I measured it three times with three different Oreos. I can confirm all three Oreos tasted great. I mean…they were all properly calibrated to match the display.

Finally, from a battery chart standpoint, here’s where things stand:

Just to quickly cover this chart with my real-world testing. When it comes to daily battery life, I’m seeing roughly 4-6 days in the real world (which is inclusive of 1-2 hours of GPS workouts per day).

For the workout claims, I’m simply not getting anywhere near those results. They claim 30 hours in always-on display mode with Max GPS, yet I’m consistently under 20 hours, sometimes low 20 hours. For running, they’re saying it may be a bug with the GPS subsystem. For cycling, it’s also been consistently estimated at 20 hours. In cycling, they say that’s because of a bug in how the device goes into Bluetooth accessory scanning mode each time I stop (including even at stop lights/stop signs), searching again for any sensors it can’t find (such as those for other bikes). As a result, in cycling mode it’s barely achieving an estimated 20 hours of battery life. COROS says they plan an update in November to address this.

With that, let’s dive into the daily basics!

The Basics:

In this section, I’ll cover all the daily basics of using the watch. Things like the hardware, user interface, activity/sleep tracking, and more. Then after that we’ll dive into all the sports bits, following which I’ll cover the accuracy of the new heart rate sensor, as well as GPS accuracy.

Starting off with the hardware aspects, the unit has three buttons, with one of them being the Digital Crown. On the left side you’ve got a button that opens up a quick-access control panel (for enabling/disabling things like sleep mode, or satellite modes, speaker volume, etc.). This was previously the Action Button on other recent watches, but now it is more…ummm…actionable. During activities it switched to the map page.

Meanwhile, on the right side, there’s the Digital Crown for scrolling through menus (and pressing enter to start a workout), as well as the lower right button, which acts as a ‘back/escape’ option.  You can long-hold the lower right button to get to the controls menu.

As for the Digital Crown, as always I like them for scrolling in maps, but otherwise I find them finicky on a sports watch. This includes on Apple Watches just as much as COROS watches. That said, with the touch screen on the COROS watch, I’ll generally use that for getting around menus instead, so it’s mostly a wash here.

Next, the Pace 4 Pro has a much brighter 3,500 nit display – by far the brightest display from COROS. Do keep in mind though, that every company advertises *peak* brightness, not actual constant brightness levels, which are variable based on the ambient light sensor. No company can maintain an AMOLED display at 3,500 nits constantly without slaughtering the battery and display life.

That said, it’s also unnecessary to do so. I live on an island in the Mediterranean, where it’s bright and sunny, and I have no issues seeing the Pace 4 Pro in any lighting conditions (including bright sunny days), and most of the time I can tell it’s clearly not at 3,500 nits (because even 1,500 nit watches are more than enough for sunny days).

Here’s the Pace 4, Pace Pro, and Pace 4 Pro side-by-side in direct sunlight:

In the above case, all units were set to their default brightness settings of ‘Standard’ (there are three levels: Standard/High/Max). Point being, even on the lowest level, I had no issues at all.

Now, one nifty thing here is the new battery usage feature COROS recently added to their app. This lets you see what drives battery level for each function. The problem is, as nifty as this is, it’s also hilariously wrong when it comes to sport usage. I’d argue it’s heavily misleading, though I think that misleading aspect is more engineering geekery than purposeful deceit. The reason is that the % listed next to the activity level is incorrect. Instead, it’s *only* looking at the GPS function specifically, not the processing pieces, which get bundled under ‘General Use’ and ‘Daily Features’, making it seem far higher in GPS time than reality.

So, let’s look at today’s run I just did (90 mins). In this case, looking at the battery chart, it shows a mere 2.6% above.

But in reality, you can see the before/after photos I took, where the battery went from 69% to 61%:

Since the beginning of watch time (including COROS’s own GPS battery claim chart shown above), you’d list this as 8% battery loss. Not 2.6% battery loss. I brought this up to COROS (for a different workout/ride), and it sounds like some changes might be on the way, with them saying:

“Lastly, sorting out the battery health / usage topic with our PM now and we are sorting out a way to display battery drain for an activity with sub-items all from within the activity usage, so in your example you would see 15% as the total activity amount rather than 8% for the activity, and the other 7% placed under other categories.”

Hopefully that’ll happen, as the feature is actually really really cool, and better than anything else out there for sports watches (Apple has some elements of this on the app, and Garmin has most aspects of this on the watch, but COROS implements it better UI-wise long-term in the app).

Nonetheless, moving along, here’s the stock watch face. As with other COROS watches, you can customize plenty of it within the watch itself, or from the COROS app:

Sliding down from there are the widgets. Each widget glance of sorts can be opened up to see more details about it. For example, here’s the daily activity widget showing today’s activity details, and then if I crack that open, I can get those metrics trended over 7 days:

Scrolling down from there, there’s a handful of others as well. I can customize these, including whether they appear, as well as the order:

Of course, one of them is sleep metrics. Here I can see my sleep summary details, as well as my deeper stats like sleep phase/stage time.

All of this is also displayed on the COROS App, including newly revamped sleep pages with sleep score details, and tons more sleep data. Or at least, the presentation of the data is improved.

Additionally, in the event you take a nap, COROS will show nap details. In fact, I really like the way they show your different sleep bits on a single page, and even offer the ability to merge things together. Like, for example, two days ago when I went to bed too late, then we had some bonkers-crazy thunderstorms in the middle of the night that kept all the kids up for a bit. Point being, by the time I got back from school drop-off rounds, I just went back to sleep for 90 minutes.

As for the accuracy of these metrics, I focus specifically on the times I went to sleep and woke up. And these have been mostly spot-on, though, last night wasn’t great. I don’t compare sleep phase/stages, because that’s mostly fake-science for clicks. The accuracy of those metrics from so-called gold-standard methodologies is only about 80% accurate. So trying to compare one device to something that’s at best 80% accurate isn’t super helpful to anyone. Thus, I won’t waste your time with that.

Instead, if we look at last night, for example, here’s how things handled (I was reading on my phone for a while):

Feel Asleep (Actual): ~12:50-12:55AM
COROS Pace 4 Pro: 12:01AM
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 12:50AM
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 11:56PM
Whoop 5.0/MG: 12:52AM
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 12:55AM
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 1:03AM

Woke Up (Actual): Alarm at 7:50AM, snoozed to 7:58AM
COROS Pace 4 Pro: 7:58AM
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 7:58AM
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 8:00AM
Whoop 5.0/MG: 7:56AM
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 7:58AM
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 7:49AM

Next, one of the metrics it’ll capture while you’re sleeping is your overnight HRV. It’ll trend this over time after you’ve established your baseline metrics, showing things like ‘Normal’ or outside of ranges:

Here’s how that compared last night:

COROS Pace 4 Pro: 64ms
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 66ms
Garmin Cirqa (Bicep): 63ms
Whoop 5.0/MG: 63ms
Amazfit Helio (Bicep): 68ms
Fitbit Air (Bicep): 55ms

As you can see, virtually all of them are the same. Save the Fitbit Air, which I find consistently low for whatever reason.

Now, all of these metrics (HRV, sleep, activity, etc.) are pulled into the COROS app on your smartphone, where you can view them and dig into more details for any of them. You can also adjust these tiles as you see fit:

Next, switching topics, at this juncture COROS has yet to implement a real LED flashlight into their watches. Still, they do offer a simplistic screen-based flashlight. And given the brighter 3,500-nit display, it works just fine.

That said, I’m really hoping COROS joins the Flashlight Club (which currently contains Garmin, Suunto, and Amazfit). It’s just more practical to have the flashlight pointed at the thing you’re trying to illuminate, rather than illuminating my own face.

Now when it comes to music, note that the COROS Pace 4 Pro does have music storage on it, but realistically you probably won’t use it. It supports downloading MP3 files, and then pairing up your headphones via Bluetooth. But of course, in 2026 almost nobody is doing that. They’re instead using platforms like Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, etc., which COROS doesn’t support (certainly COROS would love to support those platforms, but those major platforms have largely gatekept their services).

That said, you can control music/media on your phone, such as podcasts or any other platform:

Oh, and lastly, there’s the voice control bits. There’s actually a few different features that leverage the microphone, both in workout mode (like saving voice notes), as well as afterwards for saving workout notes. But in regular mode, you can also use it to simply use your watch to open things. Just long-press the lower left button. For example, you can ask it to start a run:

Now, as I’ve said on countless other watches, I’m not really a ‘talk to my wrist’ guy. And especially not a ‘it takes longer to talk to my wrist and wait than just press the darn button twice’ kinda guy. I’m sure down the road years from now this sort of thing will be faster and more useful, but these days it’s mostly a gimmick to me. Nonetheless, to each their own!

With that, let’s head out for a workout.

Sports Usage:

Next up, if you’re buying a COROS watch, you’re almost certainly doing so for some sort of sports usage. So in this section I’m gonna go through all those pieces, including during workouts, post-workout training load and recovery pieces, as well as a bit of offline mapping and navigation components. To be clear, absolutely nothing here has changed since any other recent COROS watch (which are all running essentially the same software). Instead, the changes around sport usage mainly come from heart rate accuracy, which I cover in the next section.

In any case, the first step is choosing a sport mode. The COROS Pace 4 Pro has virtually all the major sport modes you’d expect. It’s not quite the Girls Gone Wild listing of some 200 sports modes of Amazfit, but it gets the job done. The main ones you’d be missing compared to some of COROS’s higher-end watches are around climbing (e.g., rock climbing). But if heights aren’t your jam, then you won’t miss anything here.

In any case, to select a sport mode, you’ll tap the upper right button and scroll through the sport modes to find your pain:

Once you’ve done that, it’ll go off and find GPS (if outdoors), as well as any sensor accessories (such as cycling power meters or an external heart rate sensor). It’s here that you can select things like structured workouts, basic interval workouts, and apply a route for navigation. Or just tweak other sport settings.

In our case for today’s run, I’m going to load up a route/course. I created this route in Strava, which then pushed to my COROS account. Though (still) annoyingly, COROS doesn’t automatically transfer that to my watch. I’ll need to go into the COROS app and then select to push it to the watch. I know I’ve harped on this for years, but when it comes to tiny features that are actually helpful to athletes, just syncing the darn route is so much more useful than voice prompts.

Once I send it to the watch, it appears here to select, along with some quick stats about the run:

You can also, of course, create routes on other platforms, import GPX files, and create routes within the COROS app as well (including creating waypoints).

Once all that is sorted, out we go for our run. While running, you’ll see the data pages as you’ve configured them. All of this is pretty straightforward:

When it comes to that route, you’ll see your route overlaid atop the map, and then get turn notifications ahead of each turn (about 50m away while running/hiking, a bit further while cycling). It’ll indicate which way to turn:

If you go off-route, then the watch will let you know within about 50m as well. Note that the COROS watches don’t support offline re-routing. It’ll simply let you know which compass direction the actual route is, and it’s up to you to figure that out.

You can also see your elevation profile of the planned route, and other handy stats:

Plus, automatic climb details will engage as you hit a climb:

In the event you want to create a voice note, pinned to the location, for later inclusion in your workout journal, you can do that via the controls menu. These will then show up as notes (with your voice note using the microphone) on the journal and workout track. Again, it’s not really my jam, but I know people who do find the voice notes useful for scouting things. Note the play button below, and then the automatic transcription (I include the actual audio in my review).

Once your workout is complete, you’ll see all the summary stats on the watch, such as this from today’s trail run:

And you can also add yet another voice note, this time for RPE. I’ve skipped that, and just went with smiley-face style. That’s more my jam.

Then, once this all syncs to the COROS app, you can see your full workout details here; note in particular, it’ll show your voice notes on the map itself, and you can also add in photos from the workouts, which will show up accordingly in the right spots using GPS information.

When it comes to training load metrics, COROS has a basic Race Predictor feature, a Running Score feature, and Training Load metrics. Here’s the Race Predictor feature. Note that this really only takes into account flat-ground runs, and not hilly trail runs like mine. In my case, the vast majority of my runs are trail runs (and specifically, very hilly ones), so my numbers rarely get updated here.

There’s also your overall training Intensity and Recovery metrics. I find the recovery metrics reasonably close to how I’m feeling.

Next, there’s training load. And like clockwork, I’m going to complain again that this resets every single Monday. In real life, training load doesn’t reset every Monday. If you did the Berlin Marathon on Sunday, you still very much have that training load in your legs Monday morning (as any staircase will remind you). Yet for COROS, it all disappears. Here’s my Sunday night:

And then the next day it’s zero. Sigh.

I’m hoping if I keep banging this drum, COROS will finally change it. They did on the smartphone app, but not yet on the watches. Eventually?

Heart Rate & GPS Accuracy:

First, let’s look at a lazy interval workout yesterday; you can see that overall it’s mostly good. There’s one minor error early on for a few seconds, then it sorts itself out. Along with some slight delays coming down from intervals towards the end (as I’d start the walk), though neither is a massive deal. Also very, very slight delays on the start of some intervals, but nothing you’d likely notice in real life.

Next, we’ve got a harder interval workout at the track. Now, in this case I had a Polar H10 chest strap with me, though apparently it was on its last battery legs, and created a proper mess of things, as you can see below. Still, as for the COROS itself, it happily agreed with all the other devices on this journey, which is good. And if I sift through the mess below, I don’t see any cases where the COROS Pace 4 Pro is out of line here.

Next, some indoor trainer high-intensity intervals. From a cycling standpoint, these 30-second intervals went from 150w to 590w, and were probably the most visible case of delays with the optical HR sensor. You can see it took quite a while to catch up:

That said, for these sorts of high-intensity intervals, the delay of the HR being a few seconds late isn’t usually something most coaches (or analytics aspects) would look at. That’s because HR itself (your actual heart) is a lagging indicator for effort here. Instead, using pace or power is what actually matters here. And you can see in the second half when I lowered the intensity a bit, it was much faster to catch up.

Meanwhile, on this other trainer ride, which was following a virtual route where things were a bit more civil, the two lines are reasonably close. There are some minor quirks coming down from high-intensity moments, where you see a bit of bobble in the HR. Nothing massive, but something that could use a bit of work. Also note the colors are flipped here, just…sigh…because.

The same goes here with another trainer ride. On the whole it’s pretty darn good (though remember, trainer rides are like the easiest thing ever for optical HR sensors). Still, there are some minor mistakes here that could use some work. This kinda vaguely reminds me of Polar’s HR mini-spike/bobbling-drop issues on most of their recent wristwatches.

And then switching to the opposite end of the spectrum in terms of difficulty for optical HR sensors to track, is an outdoor ride. Here we can see that, on the whole, it’s got the gist of things. But we can also see numerous errors/offsets, especially at higher intensities when things are normally stable. This is actually fairly unusual. Usually for outdoor cycling, once you reach a higher intensity, heart rate readings tend to become easier for devices to track. It’s the transition phase (easy to hard, hard to easy) that most wearables in rougher conditions mess up.

In any case, looking at the new optical HR sensor, I’d argue it is improved over the previous generation, but equally, other companies are also improving. And I’d say those other companies’ pace of improvement is faster than COROS here. Which isn’t to say the above is bad. It’s certainly not. But rather, the bar has been raised, and while COROS has made improvements, their overall place in the standings stays roughly at the upper end of the mid-tier. But it’s far from industry-leading.

Meanwhile, for GPS I’m simply not seeing anything that’s concerning at this point across running (trail running and road running), as well as cycling. For example, a trail run today (in ‘High’, but not ‘Max’), and things are virtually identical to the Fenix 9 Pro:

I’ve got some other watches in this test, but you’ll have to wait till next week for those. Either way, they all match here.

Here’s another trail run, this time versus the Amazfit Dual Solar watch (and Garmin Fenix 9 Pro), at the ‘Auto’ level, all looks well:

Though, you can see in the trails that the COROS Pace 4 Pro easily outperforms the Amazfit unit, which was frequently off in the bushes. I only spend time in the bushes when I need to collect a crashed drone, and this wasn’t one of those times.

Here’s an interval run we did on the streets. Over and over again loops. Loops like this are always fun for repetition purposes on GPS tracks. Again, at a high level it all looks good:

That said, looking closely here, I do see a slight offset by the COROS on this stretch. Again, merely the wrong side of the street, so not a massive deal. Though, consistently the wrong side every loop. The others were correct (we ran down the left side of this deserted street).

Setting aside this street/turn, on the whole I think the COROS Pace 4 Pro has perfectly functional GPS accuracy. As I noted earlier, I remain a bit concerned about the battery burn during GPS workouts, due to bugs COROS says are lingering, causing that battery to be substantially higher than it should be. COROS says fixes are coming in the November timeframe, but as always with GPS vs. battery fixes, there’s usually a tradeoff. Especially in cases like the Auto one where COROS says it’s switching too frequently.

In any case, it’s something I’ll keep an eye out for later this fall.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

Overall, the COROS Pace 4 Pro definitely *feels* more premium. It was easily mistaken by friends as a Garmin Forerunner 570 or Forerunner 970 on my wrist numerous times. It looks a lot like it. The display is brilliant, in terms of size and clarity, as well as brightness. Likewise, the titanium bezel looks nice. All of that is good. Whether or not consumers find the $150 upsell over the existing COROS Pace Pro to be worthwhile is probably the bigger question.

COROS has argued in media presentations that it competes with the Forerunner 970. As I noted in the video, that’s simply a hard no. Not even close. On the hardware front, it lacks many of the hardware features the Forerunner 970 has (e.g., the flashlight, medically certified ECG, a much better optical HR sensor, better GPS accuracy, and more). And then on the software side, it’s not even close, no matter which software category you choose. Garmin dominates there (very deeply).

However, compared to the Forerunner 570? That’s fresh meat for the taking. Priced $100 more at $549, the Forerunner 570 lacks offline maps, lacks a flashlight, and lacks ECG. Yes, the Forerunner 570 is an excellent sports/running watch if you exclude those features, and is deeper in most (all?) of the non-mapping sports categories than COROS is. But it’s a price tradeoff that it seems many people are willing to take. COROS is better served to focus on that battle.

But whether those same consumers are willing to pay substantially more than the Pace 4 or Pace Pro for nearly the same software? Now that’s a bigger COROS-focused question that only time will tell. History has spoken loud and clear (repeatedly) that COROS is most deadly when they focus on budget. Though, this time it does somehow feel slightly different.

Either way, I think it’s a great-looking watch that’s coming from a company that continues to push new features to both the app and hardware roughly every quarter, and also continues to add polish to the app & watch firmware.

With that – thanks for reading!
